title: When Expressivity Is Not Enough: Discrete Routing Geometry in Variational Quantum Circuits
abstract: Finding useful variational quantum circuits requires more than representational capacity: training must also have access to directions that improve the objective. We study how discrete CNOT routing shapes both capacity and local accessibility. For circuits built from CNOT and arbitrary one-qubit gates, we separate binary routing matrices from continuous rotations to relate global capacity to local tangent accessibility. An exact finite-field formula for the operator Schmidt rank of a CNOT block and cumulative multiblock bounds yield capacity constraints and a Bell-pair fidelity obstruction. Locally, routing propagates generators into a routing-dependent tangent space, so all parameter gradients can vanish even when the ambient objective gradient is nonzero; frame bounds distinguish loss of gradient coverage from poor conditioning. A routing-conditioned identity insertion preserves the current unitary, state, loss, and existing gradients while adding new tangent directions. Candidate-only and incremental projection scores provide local criteria for ranking insertions. Exact-statevector tests show strong short-horizon score-descent correlations on controlled Bell tasks and effective equal-cost selection on connected Heisenberg chains up to twelve qubits, with complementary TFIM selector controls. A broader TFIM routing ensemble exhibits routing-dependent near-stagnation. Together, these results connect representational capacity, local accessibility, and same-point repair through a common discrete routing description. An architecture need not remain fixed during training: task-dependent geometric information can guide the opening of new descent directions while preserving the learned circuit at insertion. This provides a concrete local approach to a broader problem: how useful quantum circuits can be discovered from the information a task supplies.
summary: This work analyzes the geometric constraints on variational quantum circuits, showing that simply having enough parameters is insufficient for effective training. By focusing on the discrete routing structure of CNOT gates, the authors quantify how this geometry limits local optimization directions, proposing a method to actively guide the circuit's structure during training to ensure convergence.
main_problem: The study investigates whether training variational quantum circuits requires more than just sufficient representational capacity; the training process must also have access to directions that improve the objective function.
main_result: The paper establishes a concrete link between representational capacity, local accessibility, and the ability to repair training stagnation by analyzing the role of discrete CNOT routing geometry.
method: The authors use mathematical tools like operator Schmidt rank, finite-field formulas, and tangent space analysis to characterize the geometry of the reachable unitary set defined by the circuit's routing structure.
model_or_system: The model is a variational quantum circuit built from CNOT gates and arbitrary one-qubit gates, parameterized by a mixed encoding involving discrete routing matrices (from GL(n, F2)) and continuous rotations.
key_observables: Operator Schmidt Rank (OSRS), local gradient coverage (tangent space projection $\Pi_{T_A}$), and the ability to restore descent directions.
important_parameters: The size of the system ($n$), the number of layers ($t$), and the specific structure of the CNOT routing matrix $A$.
main_assumptions: The local results do not establish efficient global search, asymptotic barren-plateau suppression, or noisy-hardware advantage.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the mechanism: tracing reachable sets, showing ambient descent directions orthogonal to the accessible space, and demonstrating how identity-initialized routing blocks can restore descent.
paper_structure: The paper first analyzes the global constraints using OSRS and cut-rank formulas for single and multiple CNOT blocks. It then moves to local analysis, demonstrating gradient vanishing when the accessible tangent space is orthogonal to the objective gradient. Finally, it proposes and tests a 'same-point augmentation' technique to guide the opening of new descent directions.
why_interesting: It provides a deep geometric understanding of the limitations of variational quantum algorithms, suggesting that structural modifications (routing) can be used to guide optimization away from local minima or plateaus.
